planting.note: Set container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained acidic soil in full sun; this heath tolerates a touch more lime in the ground than most of its relatives but still resents heavy clay.

directions: Cornish heath forms a billowing, wiry-stemmed evergreen mound that erupts in late summer with dense spikes of small bell flowers ranging from pale pink through rose to near-white depending on the seedling. It flowers later than most hardy heaths, extending the bloom season of a heather bank into autumn when little else in the heath family is still going. Give it full sun and sharply drained, lean soil, since rich ground makes the growth lax and floppy. Shear the whole plant lightly in early spring before new growth begins to keep the mound tight and encourage the next season's flower spikes.

planting.note: Plant in spring into consistently moist, acidic, peaty soil in full sun to light shade; unlike most heaths it prefers ground that never fully dries out.

directions: Cross-leaved heath gets its name from the whorls of four grey-downy leaves set in neat crosses along each stem, topped from midsummer into fall by rounded clusters of rose-pink flowers held above the foliage. It is a true bog-edge plant, native to wet heath and moorland, so it wants consistently damp, peaty, acidic soil rather than the sharp drainage most of its relatives demand. Plant it where winter wet won't drain away entirely, such as a low spot in a heather bed or beside a rain garden. Trim lightly after flowering to keep the habit dense without cutting into old wood.

planting.note: Set container stock in spring into well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; this old Irish heath selection is more lime-tolerant than most Erica but still benefits from acidic conditions.

directions: W.T. Rackliff is a long-grown, compact Irish heath selection prized for its contrast of bright lime-green young foliage against pure white, honey-scented bell flowers that open from late winter into spring. It builds a tidy, rounded dome of growth that is denser and slower than the plain species, making it useful as a low specimen or edging shrub in a winter garden. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, where it shrugs off both cold winds and a surprising amount of garden lime for a heath. Shear immediately after flowering to maintain the compact shape and encourage fresh foliage color.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; as the original darleyensis selection it tolerates mildly alkaline ground better than most true heaths.

directions: Darley Dale was the first named selection raised from the chance hybrid between winter heath and Irish heath, and it remains the benchmark against which later darleyensis cultivars are measured. It carries soft lilac-pink bell flowers over a long season from late autumn through spring, set against dense, dark evergreen foliage on a spreading mound. Plant it in full sun on well-drained soil, where it tolerates a wider pH range than most heaths and shrugs off winter cold without protection. Shear lightly once flowering finishes to keep the mound dense and promote the next flush of foliage.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this Eurasian alpine resents rich, wet ground far more than the North American pussytoes already in cultivation.

directions: European pussytoes forms a tight, silvery-grey mat of felted foliage studded in late spring with clusters of small, fuzzy flower heads held on short stems, white to dusty pink depending on the plant since this species is dioecious with separate male and female clones. It is the classic Eurasian rock-garden pussytoes, long grown as a drought-tough edging or path-side mat where little else will hold lean, gravelly soil. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, since wet winter soil is the main cause of failure. Shear off spent flower stems after bloom to keep the mat neat and encourage it to spread.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring and replant into lean, gravelly soil in full sun; deadhead promptly to keep the mat from thinning out.

directions: Rubra is the long-grown rosy-pink-flowered selection of European pussytoes, chosen for flower heads with noticeably deeper color than the washed-out pink or white of plain seedlings. It keeps the same tight, silver-felted foliage mat as the species, making a dense, low carpet that is especially effective threaded between paving stones or flat rocks. Grow it in full sun on lean, sharply drained soil, since any richness or winter wet quickly rots the crown. Trim off faded flower stems after bloom to tidy the planting and keep the mat from opening up in the center.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the soil surface since it needs light to germinate, then set out transplants into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade where summers stay mild.

directions: Himalayan blue poppy produces some of the purest sky-blue flowers in the perennial border, carried singly or a few per stem above a basal rosette of bristly, blue-green leaves, and it is generally considered showier and more reliably perennial than the related species it is often confused with. It demands cool, humid summers, consistently moist but well-drained humus-rich soil, and shelter from hot afternoon sun, which is why it thrives in the Pacific Northwest and similar maritime climates but struggles elsewhere. Sow seed shallowly since it needs light to germinate, and keep seedlings cool and evenly moist while they establish. Mulch the crown lightly over winter in colder zones to protect it from alternating freeze-thaw.
